title: Tŷ Mawr — The Great House Farm Story
description: The true story of the Williams/Buckler family and Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough-juxta-Penarth, told scene by scene in date order, with the evidence for every scene. Each scene gives what happened, the received account and its wording, and what we now know; every scene links to its evidence on the Great House Farm Wiki.
ordering: Scenes are in strict date order by "date" (ISO 8601; null for the two present-day epilogue scenes, which come last). "ref" is act.scene, "order" the running number.

entries.title: St Dochdwy's church
entries.narration: St Dochdwy's church stands at Llandough, on the site of an early monastery. Great House stands beside it.
entries.received_account: A village church with a farm next to it.
entries.what_we_now_know: One of the oldest Christian sites in Wales, and the ground beside it the site of the largest early medieval cemetery yet found in Wales. The house next to it was the manor's house, not an ordinary farmhouse.

entries.title: Medieval occupation
entries.narration: Pottery of the 12th to 14th centuries is later found on the slope north-east of the house. The Royal Commission classes the house as sub-medieval, probably 17th century.

received_wording.note: A technical dating term, later read as "not old enough to matter".

entries.what_we_now_know: A house of the 17th century or earlier, on a site occupied since the Middle Ages, possibly with a medieval core.

entries.title: The Williams family at Great House
entries.narration: Mary Williams's statement (c. 1974) records her family at Great House from 1667.

title_ledger.Great House (one farm): Freehold: the Vaughans · in the house: the Williamses

entries.received_account: Tenant farmers who lived on someone else's land.

received_wording.note: The estate's description of the family, repeated in every later account.

entries.what_we_now_know: For more than three hundred years one family lived in the house where the manor's courts sat, beside one of the oldest churches in Wales. Generation after generation was born there, married there and died there. Mary's account is that her ancestors bought it. Whatever the estate's books called them, the Williamses were the people of the Great House. Not squatters. Not passing tenants. The family of the house.

entries.narration: Mary Williams's statement records that in 1877 the Bute Estate sold the farmhouse, buildings and about 10 acres to Daniel Thomas, and kept about 9 acres. The Williamses remained as tenants of both. The deed is missing.

entries.received_account: Nothing changed: Bute went on owning the farm, and the Williamses went on renting it.
entries.what_we_now_know: From 1877 there are two parcels with two owners: Parcel A, the house, owned by Thomas; Parcel B, the fields, owned by Bute. Anything Bute sells after 1877 can only be Parcel B. And the bargain made with a family who had already lived there for two hundred years was that when the quarrying ended, the house would be theirs.

entries.received_account: If the family ever had documents, they could not produce them.

received_wording.said: "No such documents were, however, ever produced."

entries.what_we_now_know: Imagine it. The papers that proved your home was yours, kept safe in a blanket box for generations, carried out of the house by a stranger an estate agent had put under your roof. It happened a year after Mary relied on them, and within three years of the landlord's first court case. For the rest of her life she was told to produce documents that had been taken from her. The title was never extinguished. Only its proof was taken.

entries.title: The 1955 possession order
entries.narration: On 2 February 1955 Western Ground Rents obtains a High Court order for possession against Frederick Buckler, described as "the whole of the farm". On 4 July 1955 possession is taken of everything except the farmhouse and garden. Mary Williams had recently returned from hospital.

entries.received_account: The landlord recovered the farm in 1955; the family stayed on in the house only through the landlord's forbearance, and from 1955 their occupation was adverse to the landlord.

received_wording.note: The clock the courts later counted on the house.

entries.what_we_now_know: An order against a tenant of the fields can only give back the fields, and that is what was taken. On the family's account the woodland went too, to a couple in Llandough and later to a charity. Mary was not a party and was never heard. She had just come home from hospital, having lost a leg, to find the landlord's men taking the farm around her, and she stood her ground for her house. Any clock that started in 1955 was a clock on the fields. That the order reached the house was an insinuation, later read as fact.

entries.received_account: A landlord and its successors recovered their farm from tenants who stayed on without paying, and the courts confirmed it.
entries.what_we_now_know: Parcel A was the family's from 1928, and by possession from 1940. It was never shown to belong to Western Ground Rents or BP. A synthetic single farm was described in 1916; six attempts (1949, 1955, 1959, 1962, 1965, 1974) treated Mary's occupation as permissive; the woodland and the land to the south were taken; the 1975 conveyance and 1983 registration gave the synthetic Parcel A a deed and a title; the 1987 amalgamation folded it into Parcel B. The courts decided possession and never decided ownership. Possession can be awarded without ownership being tried, and land can be registered without a rival claim being decided.
